title: EU Approves $110 Billion Paramount-Warner Bros Merger as US Review Continues

author.name: Michael Chen
author.bio: Michael Chen covers media mergers, acquisitions, and the entertainment industry.

image: /images/news/EU Approves $110 Billion Paramount-Warner Bros Merger as US Review Continues.webp
excerpt: The European Commission has approved the proposed $110 billion merger between Paramount Global and Warner Bros. Discovery, though the landmark media deal remains under regulatory review in the United States.

content.text: The European Union has approved the proposed $110 billion merger between Paramount Global and Warner Bros. Discovery, removing one of the biggest regulatory hurdles facing what would become one of the largest media and entertainment companies in the world. The European Commission concluded that the transaction would not significantly reduce competition within the European Economic Area after conducting an in-depth assessment of the companies' television, film, streaming, and advertising businesses.

While the decision represents a major milestone for the deal, the merger remains on hold as regulators in the United States continue their own antitrust review, where approval is considered far less certain.

If completed, the merger would reshape the global entertainment industry by combining two of Hollywood's most recognizable studios and content libraries under a single corporate structure. The combined company would own an extensive portfolio of television networks, streaming platforms, movie studios, sports broadcasting rights, and thousands of intellectual property assets. Paramount contributes globally recognized brands including Paramount Pictures, CBS, Nickelodeon, MTV, Comedy Central, Showtime, and the Paramount+ streaming platform. Warner Bros. Discovery brings together Warner Bros. Pictures, HBO, HBO Max, CNN, Discovery Channel, DC Studios, Cartoon Network, Eurosport, and numerous other international media properties. Together, the companies would create one of the world's largest producers and distributors of entertainment content.

Executives behind the merger argue that greater scale has become essential as traditional media companies compete against technology giants such as Netflix, Amazon, Apple, Disney, and YouTube for viewers, advertising revenue, and streaming subscribers. The rapid shift from traditional cable television toward on-demand streaming has fundamentally transformed the economics of the entertainment business.

Building and maintaining global streaming platforms requires billions of dollars in annual investments in original programming, technology infrastructure, marketing, and international expansion. Supporters of the merger believe combining resources would allow the companies to compete more effectively in an increasingly crowded global marketplace while generating significant operational efficiencies.

The European Commission's investigation examined whether the combined company could unfairly restrict competitors' access to television programming, sports broadcasting rights, film distribution, advertising markets, or streaming services. Regulators ultimately concluded that sufficient competition would remain across Europe's media landscape, citing the continued presence of numerous international streaming platforms, broadcasters, and production companies. The Commission also noted that consumers would continue having access to a wide variety of entertainment providers, reducing concerns that the merger would substantially lessen competition within European markets. The decision reflects the EU's broader approach of evaluating whether mergers directly harm consumer choice rather than simply focusing on company size.
US Regulators Take a Closer Look

Attention now shifts to the United States, where federal regulators are conducting a far more detailed review of the proposed transaction. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the Department of Justice have adopted a more aggressive stance toward major corporate mergers in recent years, particularly those involving technology, telecommunications, and media companies.

U.S. authorities are expected to closely examine whether combining two major Hollywood studios could reduce competition for television programming, streaming services, film production, advertising sales, and sports broadcasting rights. Analysts believe regulators may also consider how the merged company's increased negotiating power could affect cable providers, streaming distributors, advertisers, and independent content producers.

The merger arrives during a period of significant financial pressure across the global media industry. Traditional television networks continue losing subscribers as audiences increasingly migrate toward streaming platforms and digital content. At the same time, media companies face rising production costs, intense competition for premium content, and slowing advertising growth in several markets.

Investors have increasingly demanded that entertainment companies improve profitability after years of heavy spending on streaming expansion. Many industry observers believe further consolidation is inevitable as media groups seek larger subscriber bases, stronger content libraries, and greater economies of scale to remain competitive against global technology platforms.
Streaming Services at the Core of Future Strategy

Streaming services are expected to play a central role in the combined company's future strategy. Paramount+ and HBO Max together would create one of the world's largest subscription streaming businesses, offering an enormous catalog of films, television series, live sports, documentaries, children's programming, and original productions. Executives have suggested that combining streaming operations could reduce technology costs, improve content recommendations, strengthen international distribution, and accelerate subscriber growth.

However, integrating two large digital platforms presents substantial operational challenges, including harmonizing technology systems, subscription models, licensing agreements, and global branding strategies.

Financial markets responded cautiously to the European approval. Investors generally welcomed progress toward completing the merger but remained focused on the outcome of the U.S. regulatory review, which many analysts consider the decisive stage of the transaction. Media industry experts note that regulatory scrutiny of large mergers has intensified globally as governments become increasingly concerned about market concentration, consumer choice, and competition within digital industries. Even if U.S. regulators ultimately approve the transaction, they could require asset sales, behavioral commitments, or other conditions designed to preserve competition in specific markets.

Beyond regulatory considerations, successfully integrating two multinational media organizations would represent one of the largest corporate combinations in entertainment history. The merged company would need to align business operations, corporate cultures, production strategies, technology platforms, and international distribution networks while continuing to compete aggressively in a rapidly evolving industry. Analysts estimate that the companies could realize billions of dollars in annual cost savings through operational efficiencies, although achieving those benefits would likely require significant restructuring over several years.

The European Union's approval marks a significant step forward for the proposed $110 billion transaction, but the future of the deal now depends largely on decisions made by U.S. regulators. If approved, the merger would fundamentally reshape the competitive landscape of the global media industry, creating a new entertainment powerhouse with unmatched content assets and worldwide reach. Until then, investors, competitors, and consumers will be closely watching the American regulatory process, which is expected to determine whether one of the biggest media mergers in history ultimately moves forward or faces additional delays.
